prompt:
Let $p$ be a prime of the form $p=4n-1$ where $n$ is a positive integer. Prove that
$$\prod_{k=1}^p(k^2+1)\equiv4\pmod p.$$
answer: The squares $k^2$ run over $0$ (once) and every quadratic residue $r$ (twice), and $\prod_r(x-r)\equiv x^{(p-1)/2}-1$; at $x=-1$ this gives $\prod_r(r+1)\equiv2$, so the product is $\equiv 2^2=4$.

solutions.title: Quadratic residues as roots of $x^{(p-1)/2}-1$
solutions.body:
All congruences are modulo $p$. As $k$ runs over $1,\dots,p$ (a complete residue system), $k^2$ takes the value $0$ once ($k=p$) and each of the $\frac{p-1}2$ nonzero quadratic residues exactly twice ($\pm k$). Let $Q$ be the set of nonzero quadratic residues. Then
$$\prod_{k=1}^p(k^2+1)\equiv1\cdot\prod_{r\in Q}(r+1)^2 .$$

**Claim:** $\prod_{r\in Q}(x-r)\equiv x^{(p-1)/2}-1$ as polynomials over $\mathbb Z_p$. Indeed every $r=s^2\in Q$ satisfies $r^{(p-1)/2}=s^{p-1}\equiv1$ (Fermat), so the $\frac{p-1}2$ distinct elements of $Q$ are roots of the monic polynomial $x^{(p-1)/2}-1$ of the same degree over the field $\mathbb Z_p$, hence it factors as $\prod_{r\in Q}(x-r)$.

Put $x=-1$. Since $\frac{p-1}2=2n-1$ is odd,
$$\prod_{r\in Q}(-1-r)\equiv(-1)^{2n-1}-1=-2,$$
and $\prod_{r\in Q}(-1-r)=(-1)^{|Q|}\prod_{r\in Q}(1+r)=-\prod_{r\in Q}(r+1)$. Therefore $\prod_{r\in Q}(r+1)\equiv2$ and
$$\prod_{k=1}^p(k^2+1)\equiv2^2=4\pmod p.\ ∎$$

solutions.title: Factor $k^2+1$ over $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ (official idea)
solutions.body:
Since $p\equiv3\pmod4$, $-1$ is not a square mod $p$, so adjoin $i$ with $i^2=-1$ to get the field $\mathbb F_{p^2}=\mathbb F_p(i)$. Over any field containing $\mathbb F_p$ we have the polynomial identity
$$\prod_{k\in\mathbb F_p}(x-k)=x^p-x ,$$
because the $p$ elements of $\mathbb F_p$ are roots of $x^p-x$ (Fermat).

Now $k^2+1=(k-i)(k+i)=(i-k)(-i-k)$, so
$$\prod_{k=1}^p(k^2+1)=\prod_{k\in\mathbb F_p}(i-k)\cdot\prod_{k\in\mathbb F_p}(-i-k)=(i^p-i)\big((-i)^p+i\big).$$
As $p=4n-1$, $i^p=i^{4n}i^{-1}=-i$ and $(-i)^p=-i^p=i$. Hence the product is $(-2i)(2i)=-4i^2=4$. ∎

prompt: If we write the sequence AAABABBB along the perimeter of a circle, then every word of the length $3$ consisting of letters A and B (i.e. AAA, AAB, ABA, BAB, ABB, BBB, BBA, BAA) occurs exactly once on the perimeter. Decide whether it is possible to write a sequence of letters from a $k$-element alphabet along the perimeter of a circle in such a way that every word of the length $l$ (i.e. an ordered $l$-tuple of letters) occurs exactly once on the perimeter.

solutions.title: Eulerian circuit in the de Bruijn graph
solutions.body:
**Yes, always** (such a circular sequence is a *de Bruijn sequence*). If $l=1$, write each letter once. If $k=1$, a circle with the single letter works trivially. Let $k\ge2$, $l\ge2$, and let $P$ be the alphabet.

**The graph.** Let $G$ be the directed graph whose vertices are the $k^{l-1}$ words of length $l-1$, with an arc from $a_1a_2\dots a_{l-1}$ to $a_2\dots a_{l-1}c$ for every letter $c$. Arcs correspond bijectively to words of length $l$: the arc above corresponds to $a_1a_2\dots a_{l-1}c$. (Loops such as $AA\dots A\to AA\dots A$ are allowed.)

- Every vertex has out-degree $k$ (choice of $c$) and in-degree $k$ (arcs come from $c\,a_1\dots a_{l-2}$).
- $G$ is strongly connected: from $a_1\dots a_{l-1}$ we reach any $b_1\dots b_{l-1}$ in $l-1$ steps by appending $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_{l-1}$ one at a time.

By Euler's theorem for directed graphs, $G$ has an Eulerian circuit: a closed walk $v_0\to v_1\to\dots\to v_N=v_0$ using every arc exactly once, $N=k^l$.

**The circular word.** Let $c_j$ be the last letter of $v_j$ and write $c_1c_2\dots c_N$ around the circle (indices mod $N$). Each step shifts the word left by one and appends $c_j$, so (walking around the circuit repeatedly) $v_j=c_{j-l+2}\dots c_j$ for every $j$. Hence the $l$ consecutive letters ending at position $j$ are $c_{j-l+1}c_{j-l+2}\dots c_j=v_{j-1}c_j$, which is exactly the word of the $j$-th arc. The $N$ windows of length $l$ on the circle are therefore precisely the $N=k^l$ arcs, each used once, i.e. every word of length $l$ occurs exactly once.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

prompt:
Let $m,n$ be positive integers and let $x\in[0,1]$. Prove that
$$(1-x^n)^m+\big(1-(1-x)^m\big)^n\ge1.$$
answer: Colour each cell of an $m\times n$ board black with probability $x$ independently: \"some row is all black\" and \"some column is all white\" are disjoint events with probabilities $1-(1-x^n)^m$ and $1-(1-(1-x)^m)^n$.

solutions.title: A random colouring of a board
solutions.body:
Consider a board with $m$ rows and $n$ columns. Colour every cell black with probability $x$ and white with probability $1-x$, independently.

- A fixed row ($n$ cells) is all black with probability $x^n$; so the probability that **no** row is all black is $(1-x^n)^m$, and the event $R$ = "some row is all black" has $P(R)=1-(1-x^n)^m$.
- A fixed column ($m$ cells) is all white with probability $(1-x)^m$; it contains a black cell with probability $1-(1-x)^m$; all columns contain a black cell with probability $(1-(1-x)^m)^n$. So the event $C$ = "some column is all white" has $P(C)=1-(1-(1-x)^m)^n$.

$R$ and $C$ cannot happen together: an all-black row and an all-white column would share a cell that is both black and white. Hence
$$P(R)+P(C)=P(R\cup C)\le1,$$
i.e. $1-(1-x^n)^m+1-(1-(1-x)^m)^n\le1$, which is the claim. ∎

prompt:
Let $\mathcal B$ be a family of open balls in $\mathbb R^n$ and $c<\lambda\big(\bigcup\mathcal B\big)$ where $\lambda$ is the $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Show that there exists a finite family of pairwise disjoint balls $\{U_i\}_{i=1}^k\subseteq\mathcal B$ such that
$$\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda(U_j)>\frac{c}{3^n}.$$
answer: Vitali covering argument: take a compact $K\subseteq\bigcup\mathcal B$ with $\lambda(K)>c$, cover it by finitely many balls, and greedily pick disjoint balls by decreasing radius; the tripled chosen balls cover $K$.

solutions.title: Compactness and the greedy Vitali selection
solutions.body:
If $c<0$ the empty family works (its sum is $0>c/3^n$). Assume $c\ge0$; then $\lambda(G)>0$ for the open set $G=\bigcup\mathcal B$.

**Step 1: a compact set of measure $>c$.** For $m\ge1$ let $K_m=\{x\in G:|x|\le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus G)\ge\frac1m\}$ (with $\operatorname{dist}(x,\emptyset)=\infty$). Each $K_m$ is closed and bounded, hence compact; $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\dots$ and $\bigcup_mK_m=G$ because $G$ is open. By continuity of measure from below, $\lambda(K_m)\to\lambda(G)>c$ (also if $\lambda(G)=\infty$), so some $K=K_m$ has $\lambda(K)>c$.

**Step 2: finitely many balls.** The open balls of $\mathcal B$ cover the compact set $K$, so finitely many of them, $B_1,\dots,B_N$, already cover $K$.

**Step 3: greedy selection.** Choose $U_1$ to be a ball of largest radius among $B_1,\dots,B_N$; discard all $B_i$ that intersect $U_1$ (including $U_1$). From the remaining balls choose $U_2$ of largest radius, discard all balls meeting $U_2$, and so on until no balls remain. The chosen balls $U_1,\dots,U_k$ are pairwise disjoint.

Every $B_i$ was discarded at some step $j$, so it meets $U_j$ and its radius $r$ is at most the radius $R$ of $U_j$ (it was still available when $U_j$ was chosen). If $U_j$ has centre $z$ and $y\in B_i\cap U_j$, then every point $x$ of $B_i$ satisfies $|x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|<2r+R\le3R$. Hence $B_i\subseteq3U_j$, the ball with centre $z$ and radius $3R$.

**Step 4: conclusion.**
$$c<\lambda(K)\le\lambda\Big(\bigcup_{i}B_i\Big)\le\lambda\Big(\bigcup_{j=1}^k3U_j\Big)\le\sum_{j=1}^k3^n\lambda(U_j),$$
so $\sum_j\lambda(U_j)>c/3^n$. ∎
